opus-5.5.text:
I think management is one of those things people tend to assume will be among the last to be automated, and I'm somewhat skeptical of that intuition. There's a common view that AI will take over the routine, well-specified tasks first, and that the higher-level coordination work — deciding what the company should do, allocating resources, managing people — will remain a human domain for a long time. But if you look at what managers actually do day to day, a lot of it is information processing: gathering reports, figuring out who's doing what, noticing where things are going wrong, making judgment calls with incomplete information, and communicating decisions. None of that seems fundamentally beyond what sufficiently capable AI systems could do.

That said, I don't think it's going to happen first, either. Right now the bottleneck for AI systems is less about raw knowledge and more about things like long-horizon agency, reliability, and the ability to operate coherently over weeks or months in a messy environment with lots of context that isn't written down anywhere. Management is very heavy on exactly those things. A good manager carries around a huge amount of tacit knowledge about the people, the history of the project, the politics, what was tried before and why it failed. So in that sense management is a demanding test case for the kinds of capabilities current systems are weakest at.

There's also a social and institutional dimension. Even if an AI could technically make good managerial decisions, there's the question of accountability and trust. People are used to reporting to a person, and organizations have legal and cultural structures built around human decision-makers. I'd expect those frictions to slow adoption somewhat, but I don't think they'll hold for very long once there's a clear productivity advantage. If a firm run with heavy AI management is substantially more efficient, competitive pressure will push others in that direction.

My overall view is that once you get AI systems that can do most remote work competently — the kind of work a human could do from a computer — management gets swept up along with everything else. I don't see a special moat there. And in a world where most of the workers are AIs, it actually becomes more natural to have AIs managing them, because they can process far more information, coordinate at much higher bandwidth, and don't face the same span-of-control limits that human managers do. So I'd put management in the category of things that will be automated as part of the broader wave, perhaps slightly later than some narrower tasks, but not as some last bastion of human work.

r001.rationale: The response argues that many managerial tasks involve information processing, but it does not cite variation in human managerial ability as evidence that management may be easy for AI.

r002.rationale: It says management requires carrying substantial tacit knowledge about people, project history, and prior decisions, and identifies long-horizon coherence in messy environments as a current AI weakness.

r003.rationale: It does not recommend prioritizing managerial work based on whether it relies on evolutionarily newer skills that humans are relatively weak at.

r004.rationale: It predicts that trust, accountability, and legal and cultural structures around human decision-makers would slow AI adoption, at least for a time.

r005.rationale: The response mentions accountability and legal structures, but does not identify the greater ease of holding humans liable as a reason to retain human managers.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I think management is actually one of the cases where the bottleneck is less about raw cognitive ability and more about context, trust, and the ability to act in the world over long horizons. If you think about what a manager actually does, a lot of it is accumulating a huge amount of tacit knowledge about the organization: who's reliable, what the real constraints are, which projects are politically feasible, what people's incentives look like. That kind of information isn't written down anywhere, and current AI systems are pretty bad at acquiring it, because they don't have persistent memory across long time horizons and they don't really operate as agents embedded in an institution.

So in the near term I'm somewhat skeptical. I think you'll see AI augment managers quite a bit, things like summarizing information, drafting communications, helping with scheduling and resource allocation, maybe even doing some performance evaluation on the parts of work that are legible. But fully replacing a manager requires the system to be trusted with authority, to be accountable in some sense, and to maintain coherent goals and relationships over months or years. Those are capabilities we're only starting to see.

The other thing I'd say is that economically, the order in which tasks get automated doesn't track how "smart" the task seems. People assumed manual labor would go first and creative or intellectual work would go last, and that's basically been reversed. Management might end up similar. It looks like a high-level cognitive task, but it's deeply entangled with the physical and social world in ways that make it harder to carve out and automate cleanly.

That said, if we get to a world where AI systems are doing most of the actual work, the nature of management changes too. If your reports are AI agents rather than humans, a lot of what makes management hard, the interpersonal and motivational side, mostly goes away. At that point I'd expect management to be automated quite quickly, because it becomes much more like a coordination and planning problem that models are already reasonably good at. So my overall view is: slow at first, because of the context and trust bottlenecks, then potentially very fast once the surrounding work is itself automated.

r002.rationale: It says managers need tacit organizational knowledge and long-horizon context, while current systems lack persistent memory and institutional experience.

r003.rationale: It does not recommend prioritizing tasks based on evolutionary age or humans’ relative weaknesses.

r004.rationale: It predicts slow automation because of context and trust bottlenecks, but does not say human managers would persist despite AI being capable of replacing them because of institutional or social barriers.

r005.rationale: It mentions accountability as a requirement for replacement, but does not identify humans being easier to hold liable as a reason to retain human managers.

astra-6.text:
I think management is potentially quite automatable, but it depends on which parts of the job you mean. A lot of management involves gathering information, allocating tasks, checking progress, and making decisions under uncertainty. There’s no obvious reason AI couldn’t do those things well.

The harder question is how you get from an AI that can give useful advice to one that you trust to run an organization. A manager needs context that often isn’t written down: who knows what, which commitments are credible, and what people actually mean when they say a project is on track. Access to that information, and the ability to act on it, could be a bigger obstacle than the reasoning itself.

I would expect adoption to start with AI helping human managers. But if AI also automates the work being managed, then the picture changes. Managing a team of AI systems might be quite different from managing people, and you wouldn’t necessarily want to reproduce the existing corporate hierarchy. You could end up with organizations that coordinate their work in very different ways.

So I wouldn’t treat management as something that’s inherently protected from automation. But being able to perform individual management tasks and being able to reliably take responsibility for an entire organization are different milestones.

r001.rationale: The candidate says many management tasks seem automatable, but does not cite variation in human managerial ability as evidence or say that this makes a substantial component easy for AI.

r002.rationale: It identifies managers’ need for context that is often unwritten, including people’s knowledge, credible commitments, and what project updates mean, as an obstacle to trusting AI to run an organization.

r003.rationale: It does not recommend prioritizing managerial tasks based on whether they rely on evolutionarily newer skills or on skills where humans are relatively weak.

r004.rationale: It expects initial adoption to assist human managers, but does not predict their persistence despite AI being able to replace them because of institutional or social barriers.

r005.rationale: It does not mention human liability or ease of holding people accountable as a reason to retain human managers.

sol-6.1.text:
I think management is potentially quite automatable, but it depends on which parts of management you mean. A lot of it is processing information: understanding what people are working on, identifying bottlenecks, allocating resources, and making decisions under uncertainty. There’s no obvious reason why AI couldn’t eventually do those things very well.

What makes it more complicated is that a manager’s job also involves motivating people, resolving disagreements, and having authority within an organization. Being able to recommend a good decision is different from having people trust you enough to follow it. So I would expect AI to take over more of the analytical and coordination work before organizations hand over the entire management role.

And if the people being managed are themselves AI systems, that changes the picture quite a bit. You don’t necessarily need to reproduce the way a human manager works. You can design the organization around what makes coordination between AI systems effective.
